# Sensor and Wearable Data {#sec-sensors}

::: {.callout-note}
## What this chapter covers
Accelerometers, heart-rate monitors and continuous glucose monitors all produce
the same shape of data: one row per person per moment, for days on end. This
chapter is about what to do with that. How to handle the time axis, how to look
at the data before you summarise it, how to decide what counts as wear, how to
turn millions of minutes into a few numbers per person, and which analyses suit
the result. The examples are simulated, so everything here runs without a
device file.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup-sensors
#| include: false
library(webexercises)
```

```{r}
#| label: sensor-libs
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(slider)
```

## What makes it different

A questionnaire gives you one row per participant. A device gives you one row
per participant per epoch, for a week or two, and that changes the practical
problem in four ways.

- **Volume.** A wrist accelerometer sampling at 30 Hz for seven days is about
  18 million rows per participant before you do anything. Even summarised to
  one-minute epochs, 1,000 participants is 10 million rows.
- **Structure.** Minutes sit inside days, days sit inside people. Almost every
  mistake in this field comes from analysing one level as if it were another.
- **Time.** Nothing works until the time axis is right, and time is full of
  traps: time zones, summer time, devices whose clocks drift, files that start
  mid-afternoon.
- **Distance from the question.** Nobody asks "what was the mean acceleration?"
  They ask about *moderate-to-vigorous physical activity*, *sleep duration*,
  *time in range*. Every one of those is a construct you build from the signal
  with a chain of decisions, and the decisions matter more than the statistics
  that follow.

### The chain from signal to exposure

It is worth being explicit about that chain, because each step throws
information away and adds an assumption:

| Level | Example | Rows per person-week |
|---|---|---|
| Raw signal | acceleration on three axes at 30 Hz | ~18,000,000 |
| Epoch summary | ENMO per minute | 10,080 |
| Classified epoch | this minute counts as MVPA | 10,080 |
| Event | a 14-minute walk | tens |
| Day | 48 minutes of MVPA on Tuesday | 7 |
| Person | 41 minutes of MVPA per day on average | 1 |

Most published analyses model the last row. The work is almost entirely in
getting there, and a reader can only judge it if you describe the steps.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Decide which level your question lives at
"Are people who move more fitter?" is a person-level question: one number per
person, ordinary regression. "Do people sleep worse after an active day?" is a
day-level question *within* a person, and needs the days kept apart. "When
during the day is this group most active?" is an epoch-level question. Aggregate
to the level of the question and no further.
:::

## The example data

Real device files are large, often identifiable, and come in formats that need
a dedicated reader. So the examples here use a simulated week of wrist-worn
data: 25 participants, seven days, one-minute epochs, with an accelerometer
value and a heart rate for each minute.

The accelerometer value is **ENMO** (Euclidean Norm Minus One) in
*milli-gravity* units, mg [@vanhees2013]. It is the modern open-standard
summary of raw acceleration — the length of the acceleration vector minus 1 *g* for gravity,
averaged over the epoch and truncated at zero. A minute of sitting still is a
few mg; a brisk walk is well over 100.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How the example data were made
Worth reading once, because the structure of the simulation is the structure of
real data: a slow-moving background level, deliberate bursts of activity, and
periods when the device is not on the wrist.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-simulate
set.seed(2026)

# an AR(1) series: this is what makes activity arrive in blocks rather than
# flickering from one minute to the next
ar1 <- function(n, rho = 0.95) {
  as.numeric(stats::filter(rnorm(n, 0, 1), rho, method = "recursive"))
}

n_id <- 25
dates <- as.Date("2026-03-02") + 0:6

people <- tibble(
  id = sprintf("P%02d", 1:n_id),
  age = round(rnorm(n_id, 45, 12)),
  sex = sample(c("female", "male"), n_id, replace = TRUE),
  propensity = rnorm(n_id, 0, 0.35), # how active this person is
  resting_hr = round(60 + rnorm(n_id, 0, 7))
)

# every person-night gets its own bedtime and wake time
sleep_times <- expand_grid(id = people$id, date = dates) |>
  mutate(onset = round(rnorm(n(), 1370, 45)), offset = round(rnorm(n(), 400, 40)))

# one row per person-minute; min_of_day is an integer, so joins are exact
grid <- expand_grid(id = people$id, date = dates, min_of_day = 0:1439) |>
  left_join(people, by = "id") |>
  left_join(sleep_times, by = c("id", "date")) |>
  mutate(
    weekend = wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6,
    asleep = min_of_day < offset | min_of_day >= onset
  ) |>
  mutate(z = ar1(n()), .by = c(id, date)) |>
  mutate(z = z / sd(z), .by = c(id, date)) |>
  mutate(
    mu_base = if_else(asleep, 4, exp(3.0 + 0.55 * z + propensity)),
    k_base = if_else(asleep, 2, 3)
  )

# deliberate activity: two commutes on weekdays, exercise on some days
person_days <- distinct(grid, id, date, weekend, propensity)

bouts <- person_days |>
  mutate(exercise = rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-0.5 + 2 * propensity))) |>
  reframe(
    start = c(
      if (!weekend) round(rnorm(2, c(480, 1035), 25)) else numeric(0),
      if (exercise == 1) round(rnorm(1, 1110, 70)) else numeric(0)
    ),
    dur = c(
      if (!weekend) round(runif(2, 10, 25)) else numeric(0),
      if (exercise == 1) round(runif(1, 30, 60)) else numeric(0)
    ),
    level = c(
      if (!weekend) rep(150, 2) else numeric(0),
      if (exercise == 1) runif(1, 180, 300) else numeric(0)
    ),
    .by = c(id, date)
  ) |>
  reframe(min_of_day = start + seq_len(dur) - 1L, level = level, .by = c(id, date, start))

# The device comes off. Note that removals are sampled with a weight that
# favours the less active participants: in real studies compliance and
# behaviour go together, and that is what makes wear time a confounder.
nonwear <- bind_rows(
  person_days |>
    slice_sample(prop = 0.45, weight_by = plogis(-2.5 * propensity)) |>
    mutate(start = round(runif(n(), 420, 1150)),
           dur = round(runif(n(), 90, 420) * plogis(-propensity) * 2)),
  expand_grid(id = "P07", date = dates) |> mutate(start = 1310, dur = 130),
  expand_grid(id = c("P12", "P19"), date = dates[c(3, 6)]) |> mutate(start = 400, dur = 900),
  expand_grid(id = "P23", date = dates[5:7]) |> mutate(start = 0, dur = 1440)
) |>
  reframe(min_of_day = start + seq_len(dur) - 1L, .by = c(id, date, start)) |>
  filter(min_of_day <= 1439) |>
  distinct(id, date, min_of_day) |>
  mutate(off = TRUE)

sensor <- grid |>
  left_join(summarise(bouts, level = max(level), .by = c(id, date, min_of_day)),
    by = c("id", "date", "min_of_day")
  ) |>
  left_join(nonwear, by = c("id", "date", "min_of_day")) |>
  mutate(
    off = coalesce(off, FALSE),
    in_bout = !is.na(level),
    mu = if_else(in_bout, level, mu_base),
    k = if_else(in_bout, 25, k_base),
    enmo = round(rgamma(n(), shape = k, rate = k / mu), 1),
    # off the wrist the accelerometer still records, and reads close to zero
    enmo = if_else(off, round(runif(n(), 0, 0.3), 1), enmo),
    timestamp = as.POSIXct(paste(date), tz = "Europe/Stockholm") + min_of_day * 60
  ) |>
  arrange(id, timestamp) |>
  mutate(enmo_s = slide_dbl(enmo, mean, .before = 2, .after = 2), .by = id) |>
  mutate(
    hr = round(resting_hr + 0.85 * enmo_s^0.85 - 6 * asleep + rnorm(n(), 0, 3)),
    # the optical heart-rate sensor reports nothing at all off the wrist
    hr = if_else(off, NA_real_, hr)
  ) |>
  select(id, timestamp, date, min_of_day, enmo, hr)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: sensor-glimpse
glimpse(sensor)
```

Note what is *not* in this table: no column saying whether the device was worn,
no sleep, no activity intensity. Those are things we are about to derive.

## Time is the hard part

### Keep a timestamp and an integer

The two time columns here do different jobs. `timestamp` is a real point in
time, which you need for ordering, for durations, and for joining to anything
else. `min_of_day` is an integer from 0 to 1439, which you need whenever you
compare *times of day* across days and people.

Use the integer for that, not a decimal hour. Decimal hours are floating-point
numbers, and two routes to "8:01 in the morning" can differ in the last bits,
so joins silently fail to match:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-float
8 + 1 / 60 == 481 / 60

near(8 + 1 / 60, 481 / 60) # dplyr's tolerant comparison
```

```{r}
#| label: sensor-tod
sensor |>
  mutate(hour = min_of_day %/% 60, minute = min_of_day %% 60) |>
  slice(480:481) |>
  select(timestamp, min_of_day, hour, minute)
```

### Time zones and summer time

A device clock usually records local time, and that is where the trouble
starts. Two rules save most of the pain:

1. **Say the time zone when you parse, and never rely on the default.** The
   default is whatever the machine running the code happens to use, so the same
   script gives different answers on a colleague's laptop and on a server.
2. **Expect two broken days a year.** When the clocks change, one local day has
   23 hours and another has 25. A "daily total" is then not comparable, and a
   rule like "exclude days with fewer than 1,380 minutes of wear" quietly
   excludes everybody on one particular Sunday.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-dst
# Sweden put the clocks forward on 29 March 2026
spring <- seq(as.POSIXct("2026-03-29 00:00:00", tz = "Europe/Stockholm"),
  as.POSIXct("2026-03-30 00:00:00", tz = "Europe/Stockholm"),
  by = "1 hour"
)

length(spring) - 1 # hours in that local day

difftime(as.POSIXct("2026-03-30 00:00:00", tz = "Europe/Stockholm"),
  as.POSIXct("2026-03-29 00:00:00", tz = "Europe/Stockholm"),
  units = "hours"
)
```

The example week above deliberately avoids a clock change. Real studies do not
get that choice, so count the minutes you actually have per day rather than
assuming 1,440 (@sec-import has more on reading files; the encoding and
locale problems there are the same family of problem as this one).

### What counts as a day?

A "day" is a modelling decision, not a fact about the data, and three
definitions are in common use.

| Definition | Boundary | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Calendar day** | midnight to midnight | Daytime activity totals; anything reported per date |
| **Noon to noon** | 12:00 to 12:00 | Anything involving sleep — it keeps a night in one piece |
| **Shifted window** | e.g. 18:00 to 18:00 | Night-shift workers and day sleepers |

The noon-to-noon convention is what sleep algorithms use, for the obvious
reason that a night crosses midnight: @vanhees2015 take noon to noon as the
default and switch to 18:00-to-18:00 for participants whose sleep log shows
they fall asleep before noon. Analysed by calendar day, a night is split in
two and neither piece is a night's sleep, which is why the sleep code later in
this chapter shifts the clock by twelve hours before taking the date:

```{r}
#| eval: false
night <- as.Date(timestamp - hours(12), tz = "Europe/Stockholm")
```

The choice also changes how many days you have, because the boundaries fall in
different places:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-day-count
sensor |>
  filter(id == "P01") |>
  summarise(
    calendar_days = n_distinct(date),
    noon_to_noon_days = n_distinct(as.Date(timestamp - hours(12), tz = "Europe/Stockholm"))
  )
```

Seven calendar days become eight noon-to-noon days, because the first and last
are only half there. **Partial days at the ends are the trap**: they look like
days with very little activity, and if the wear-time rule does not remove them
they drag every average down. Always apply the valid-day rule after choosing
the boundary, never before.

::: {.callout-tip}
## State the definition, and keep one
Say in the methods which boundary you used, and use the same one throughout.
Mixing them — activity per calendar day, sleep per noon-to-noon day — is
defensible and common, but then a "day" means two different things in the same
table, and the day-level dataset cannot be joined on `date` without thought.
If you need both, carry both columns and name them so the difference is
visible.
:::

### Does the time axis have to be complete?

Device files arrive in two shapes. Some have a row for every epoch whether or
not anything was recorded; others simply stop writing when the device is idle,
charging or off, so the gaps have no rows at all. Whether that matters depends
entirely on what you do next.

**Operations that do not care about gaps.** Anything that aggregates — sums,
means, counts above a threshold, `summarise()` per day or per person — just
works. A missing row contributes nothing, which is exactly right. The same goes
for joins on a timestamp and for models fitted at day or person level.

**Operations that silently break.** Anything that counts *rows* and means
*minutes*:

- rolling windows with `slide_dbl(.before = n)`, which counts rows;
- run lengths from `consecutive_id()` or `rle()`, used for bouts and non-wear;
- `lag()` and `lead()`, which step one row, not one minute.

Here is the failure, in miniature. Two separate forty-minute still periods,
with thirty active minutes between them, and a non-wear rule of "sixty
consecutive still minutes":

```{r}
#| label: sensor-gap-demo
start <- as.POSIXct("2026-03-02 09:00:00", tz = "Europe/Stockholm")

complete_series <- tibble(
  timestamp = start + (0:109) * 60,
  enmo = c(rep(0.2, 40), rep(120, 30), rep(20, 40))
)

flag_nonwear <- function(d) {
  d |>
    mutate(still = enmo < 1) |>
    mutate(block = consecutive_id(still)) |>
    mutate(block_length = n(), .by = block) |>
    mutate(nonwear = still & block_length >= 60)
}

# the device never wrote the active minutes to the file
gappy_series <- filter(complete_series, enmo < 100)

c(
  complete = sum(flag_nonwear(complete_series)$nonwear),
  gappy = sum(flag_nonwear(gappy_series)$nonwear)
)
```

Neither still period is long enough to be non-wear, so the right answer is
zero. With the rows missing, the two periods sit next to each other, the run
counter sees eighty consecutive still rows, and eighty minutes of perfectly
good wear are thrown away. Nothing errors, and nothing in the output hints at
it.

There are two fixes. Measure the run in **time** rather than rows:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-gap-fix-time
gappy_series |>
  mutate(still = enmo < 1) |>
  mutate(block = consecutive_id(still)) |>
  mutate(
    rows = n(),
    span = as.numeric(difftime(max(timestamp), min(timestamp), units = "mins")) + 1,
    .by = block
  ) |>
  # a genuine run has as many rows as it has minutes
  mutate(nonwear = still & rows >= 60 & span == rows) |>
  summarise(nonwear_minutes = sum(nonwear))
```

Or complete the grid first, so that a missing minute is explicitly missing:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-gap-fix-complete
gappy_series |>
  complete(timestamp = seq(min(timestamp), max(timestamp), by = "1 min")) |>
  summarise(rows = n(), missing_enmo = sum(is.na(enmo)))
```

For rolling windows the same choice appears as a choice of function.
`slide_index_dbl()` takes a window in *index* units, so it cannot reach across
a gap:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-gap-rolling
gappy_series |>
  mutate(
    by_rows = slide_dbl(enmo, mean, .before = 4),
    by_time = slide_index_dbl(enmo, timestamp, mean, .before = minutes(4))
  ) |>
  slice(39:42)
```

At 10:10 the row-based window is still averaging in values from before the
half-hour gap; the index-based one is not.

::: {.callout-important}
## Fill with missing, never with zero
When you complete a grid, the new rows must be `NA`. Filling them with zero
turns "we do not know" into "the participant was perfectly still", which is the
same error as counting non-wear as sedentary time — and it is harder to spot,
because zeros look like data.
:::

### Check for gaps before you trust a count

A device can drop samples, and a file can start or end mid-day. Counting rows
per day is the cheapest possible check, and it should be the first thing you
run:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-gaps
sensor |>
  count(id, date, name = "minutes") |>
  count(minutes, name = "person_days")
```

Every person-day here has exactly 1,440 rows, so the grid is complete and the
row-counting operations later in the chapter are safe. If it were not, the two
fixes above are the options.

## Look at it before you summarise it

This is the part that gets skipped, and it is the part that catches the
problems. Three plots, in this order.

### One person, one day

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-day
#| fig-cap: "One participant, one day, at one-minute resolution. The shaded bands are the intensity cut-points used later in the chapter."
#| fig-height: 3.2
sensor |>
  filter(id == "P01", date == as.Date("2026-03-03")) |>
  ggplot(aes(min_of_day / 60, enmo)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 100, ymax = Inf,
    alpha = 0.13, fill = "firebrick") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 50, ymax = 100,
    alpha = 0.13, fill = "goldenrod") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 3), limits = c(0, 24)) +
  labs(x = "Time of day (h)", y = "ENMO (mg)", title = "P01, Tuesday")
```

You can read a day off this plot: a quiet night, a sharp burst on the way to
work, a scattered middle of the day, a bigger burst in the late afternoon. If
your plot does not look like a day, something upstream is wrong.

### Everybody, every day: the raster

This is the single most useful plot in wearable research. One row per day, time
of day along the x-axis, colour for intensity. A week of a person's life fits
in a few centimetres, and anything odd is immediately visible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-raster
#| fig-cap: "Four participants, one row per day. Dark bands are inactivity — which here is sometimes sleep and sometimes a device in a drawer."
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 9
sensor |>
  filter(id %in% c("P01", "P07", "P12", "P23")) |>
  ggplot(aes(min_of_day / 60, fct_rev(factor(date)), fill = pmin(enmo, 150))) +
  geom_raster() +
  facet_wrap(~id, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "ENMO (mg)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 3), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Time of day (h)", y = NULL)
```

Four different stories, none of which would be visible in a table of daily
means:

- **P01** wears the device all week. The nightly dark band and the twice-daily
  commute bursts are clear.
- **P07** has a dark block at the same time every evening — a habit, probably
  taking the watch off before bed.
- **P12** has two days with a long dark block right through the middle of the
  day.
- **P23** goes dark completely from the fifth day and never comes back.

The last three are not inactivity. They are a missing-data problem wearing
inactivity's clothes, and if you take daily means without dealing with them you
will conclude that P23 became extremely sedentary on Friday.

### The average day

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-profile
#| fig-cap: "Median ENMO by time of day, with the interquartile range across participants."
#| fig-height: 3.4
sensor |>
  mutate(weekend = wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6,
    bin = (min_of_day %/% 15) * 15) |>
  summarise(enmo = mean(enmo), .by = c(id, weekend, bin)) |>
  summarise(
    median = median(enmo),
    lower = quantile(enmo, 0.25),
    upper = quantile(enmo, 0.75),
    .by = c(weekend, bin)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(bin / 60, median, colour = weekend, fill = weekend)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Time of day (h)", y = "ENMO (mg)", colour = "Weekend", fill = "Weekend")
```

Note the two-step aggregation: **average within person first, then across
people**. Summarising all the rows at once would weight the people with the most
valid days most heavily, which is both wrong and invisible.

## Wear time

Everything downstream depends on deciding which minutes count. This is the
biggest methodological decision in the chapter, and it is made with code, so it
is one you can document exactly.

### Finding non-wear

The signal is not zero when the device is removed; it is *flat*. For
epoch-level data a workable rule is: a long run of minutes with almost no
movement. Long runs are what `consecutive_id()` is for — it gives a new number
every time a value changes, so a run becomes a group.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-nonwear
wear <- sensor |>
  arrange(id, timestamp) |>
  mutate(still = enmo < 1) |>
  mutate(block = consecutive_id(still), .by = id) |>
  mutate(block_length = n(), .by = c(id, block)) |>
  mutate(
    nonwear = still & block_length >= 60, # 60 minutes of near-zero
    worn = !nonwear
  ) |>
  select(-still, -block, -block_length)

wear |>
  summarise(minutes = n(), .by = nonwear) |>
  mutate(percent = round(100 * minutes / sum(minutes), 1))
```

Why a *run*, rather than a threshold on single minutes? Because sleep also
produces very low values. It is the sixty consecutive minutes of near-nothing
that distinguishes a drawer from a sleeping wrist, and a rule based on single
minutes would throw away everybody's night.

Now redraw the raster with non-wear marked, and the four stories separate
cleanly:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-raster-flagged
#| fig-cap: "The same four participants, with detected non-wear in grey. Sleep stays dark; the drawer turns grey."
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 9
wear |>
  filter(id %in% c("P01", "P07", "P12", "P23")) |>
  mutate(shown = if_else(nonwear, NA, pmin(enmo, 150))) |>
  ggplot(aes(min_of_day / 60, fct_rev(factor(date)), fill = shown)) +
  geom_raster() +
  facet_wrap(~id, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "ENMO (mg)", na.value = "grey70") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 3), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Time of day (h)", y = NULL)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Our non-wear is unrealistically obvious
In this simulation the device reads almost exactly zero when it is off, so the
rule finds it perfectly. Real non-wear is messier: a watch on a table still
picks up vibration, and the standard algorithms work on the *standard
deviation* of the raw axes over a rolling window rather than on a single
threshold. The UK Biobank processing, for example, defines non-wear as
stationary episodes of at least 60 minutes in which all three axes have a
standard deviation below 13 mg [@doherty2017]. If you are working with real files, use an established
implementation (`GGIR` for raw accelerometer data) rather than writing your
own, and report which algorithm and which parameters you used.
:::

### Valid days and who is left

With wear decided, two conventional rules follow: a day counts if it has enough
wear, and a participant counts if they have enough days.

**How many hours?** The usual figure for a waking-wear protocol is **at least
10 hours** of wear in the waking period, which is what @migueles2017 report as
the common criterion across the literature for every age group. A 24-hour
protocol like this one has to cover the night as well, so the threshold rises:
@vanhees2015 excluded nights with under 16 hours of wear. Large studies
sometimes replace the per-day rule with a coverage rule instead — the UK
Biobank analysis required at least 72 hours of wear in total *and* wear data in
every one-hour period of the 24-hour cycle, so that no time of day is
systematically missing [@doherty2017].

**How many days?** Four is the usual minimum [@migueles2017]. The basis for it
is reliability: @trost2005 concluded that "among adults, 3-5 d of monitoring is
required to reliably estimate habitual physical activity", with children and
adolescents needing more. Many protocols add "including at least one weekend
day", because weekends differ systematically — as @fig-sensor-profile showed.

Whatever you choose, apply it in code rather than by hand, and report it:

::: {.callout-note}
## These numbers are conventions, not findings
@migueles2017 attach a warning to their own recommendation table, noting that
the criteria "should be considered with caution" and that some of them need
proper testing. They are a reasonable default and a reporting standard, not a
validated threshold — which is the argument for checking whether your
conclusion survives a different one, as the second exercise at the end of this
chapter does.
:::

```{r}
#| label: sensor-valid
daily <- wear |>
  summarise(
    wear_minutes = sum(worn),
    mvpa = sum(worn & enmo >= 100),
    light = sum(worn & enmo >= 50 & enmo < 100),
    inactive = sum(worn & enmo < 50),
    mean_enmo = mean(enmo[worn]),
    .by = c(id, date)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    weekend = wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6,
    valid_day = wear_minutes >= 960 # 16 hours, for a 24-hour protocol
  )

daily |>
  summarise(valid_days = sum(valid_day), .by = id) |>
  count(valid_days, name = "participants")
```

```{r}
#| label: sensor-flow
# the participant flow, as a table you can paste into the methods
included <- daily |>
  summarise(valid_days = sum(valid_day), weekend_days = sum(valid_day & weekend), .by = id) |>
  mutate(included = valid_days >= 4 & weekend_days >= 1)

tibble(
  step = c("Participants with data", "With >= 4 valid days",
           "and >= 1 valid weekend day"),
  n = c(
    n_distinct(daily$id),
    sum(included$valid_days >= 4),
    sum(included$included)
  )
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Wear time is a confounder, not an inconvenience
People who wear the device longer accumulate more of everything. If wear time
differs between the groups you are comparing — and it usually does, because
healthier and more conscientious participants wear it longer — then any raw
daily total is partly a measure of compliance.

Three defences, in increasing order of strength: report wear time by group;
adjust for it in the model; or use a measure that is already a proportion of
wear time. None of them fixes the deeper issue, which is that the minutes you
are missing are not missing at random. They are disproportionately showers,
swimming, contact sports and nights — which is to say, not a random sample of
the behaviour you are trying to measure.
:::

## From minutes to exposures

### Cut-points, and how fragile they are

Classifying each minute by a threshold is the standard move, and the thresholds
used here — 50 mg for light, 100 mg for moderate-to-vigorous — are typical of
published wrist ENMO values for adults. They are also a choice that changes
your answer:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-cutpoint-sensitivity
tibble(cutpoint = c(80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 150)) |>
  mutate(mvpa_per_day = map_dbl(cutpoint, \(cp) {
    wear |>
      summarise(mvpa = sum(worn & enmo >= cp), .by = c(id, date)) |>
      pull(mvpa) |>
      mean()
  })) |>
  mutate(relative = round(mvpa_per_day / mvpa_per_day[cutpoint == 100], 2))
```

Twenty milli-gravity in either direction — well within the disagreement between
published cut-points — adds nearly 30% to average MVPA or removes nearly 20% of
it. That is not a reason to abandon cut-points, but it is a reason to:

- **cite the source** of the ones you use, including the wear location, age
  group and device they were derived in — a hip cut-point on wrist data is
  simply wrong;
- **report a sensitivity analysis** like the one above when the finding is
  close to a threshold;
- **be sceptical of comparisons** between studies that used different
  cut-points, different wear locations or different devices. Much of the
  variation in published activity levels is instrumentation, not populations.

### Rolling windows

Sensor signals are noisy at the epoch level, and most derived measures smooth
before deciding anything. `slider` does rolling calculations with an explicit,
readable window, and it keeps the output the same length as the input:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-rolling
#| fig-cap: "A five-minute centred rolling mean over one morning."
#| fig-height: 3
sensor |>
  filter(id == "P01", date == as.Date("2026-03-03"), between(min_of_day, 420, 600)) |>
  mutate(smoothed = slide_dbl(enmo, mean, .before = 2, .after = 2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(min_of_day / 60)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = enmo), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(aes(y = smoothed), linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Time of day (h)", y = "ENMO (mg)")
```

`.before` and `.after` are in *rows*, which is only the same as minutes if there
are no gaps — one more reason to check the grid first. `slide_index_dbl()`
windows by an index column instead, which is the safe choice with irregular
data.

### Bouts

A bout is a run of minutes above a threshold, and the same `consecutive_id()`
trick finds them. Bouts matter because ten minutes of walking is not
physiologically the same thing as ten single minutes scattered through a day,
and guidelines have historically been written in terms of bouts.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-bouts
bouts_found <- wear |>
  arrange(id, timestamp) |>
  mutate(active = worn & enmo >= 100) |>
  mutate(run = consecutive_id(active), .by = c(id, date)) |>
  summarise(
    active = first(active),
    length = n(),
    start = min(min_of_day),
    .by = c(id, date, run)
  ) |>
  filter(active, length >= 10)

bouts_found |>
  summarise(bouts = n(), minutes_in_bouts = sum(length), .by = c(id, date)) |>
  summarise(
    mean_bouts_per_day = round(mean(bouts), 2),
    mean_bout_minutes = round(mean(minutes_in_bouts), 1)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: sensor-bout-vs-total
# bouted minutes are a minority of total MVPA minutes
left_join(
  daily |> summarise(total_mvpa = sum(mvpa), .by = id),
  bouts_found |> summarise(bouted_mvpa = sum(length), .by = id),
  by = "id"
) |>
  mutate(bouted_share = bouted_mvpa / total_mvpa) |>
  summarise(across(c(total_mvpa, bouted_mvpa), sum),
    median_share = round(median(bouted_share), 2))
```

About seven in ten MVPA minutes here survive the strict bout rule. In real data
the share is usually much lower, because real activity is far more fragmented
than this simulation: incidental movement does not arrive in tidy ten-minute
blocks. Either way the number depends entirely on the definition, so the
definition belongs in the methods. Real ones usually allow a short dip below
the threshold without ending the bout, which is the first exercise at the end
of the chapter.

### Deriving the sleep period

Sleep is the clearest example of a construct built from the signal. A simple
version of the published algorithms: within each night, find the longest run of
smoothed inactivity.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-sleep
sleep <- wear |>
  arrange(id, timestamp) |>
  mutate(smoothed = slide_dbl(enmo, mean, .before = 4, .after = 5), .by = id) |>
  mutate(
    # a "night" runs from noon to noon, so it is not split at midnight
    night = as.Date(timestamp - hours(12), tz = "Europe/Stockholm"),
    inactive = worn & smoothed < 10
  ) |>
  mutate(run = consecutive_id(inactive), .by = c(id, night)) |>
  summarise(
    inactive = first(inactive),
    length = n(),
    onset = min(timestamp),
    offset = max(timestamp),
    .by = c(id, night, run)
  ) |>
  filter(inactive, length >= 120) |>
  slice_max(length, n = 1, by = c(id, night))

sleep |>
  summarise(
    nights = n(),
    median_hours = round(median(length) / 60, 2),
    iqr = round(IQR(length) / 60, 2)
  )
```

Two details carry most of the weight. The **noon-to-noon day** keeps a night
together instead of splitting it at midnight, and is the standard convention.
And `slice_max(..., by =)` picks the longest run per person-night, which is the
whole algorithm in one line.

This is a teaching version, not a validated one. Real algorithms use the
*angle* of the device rather than the magnitude of its acceleration:
@vanhees2015 estimate arm angle in a rolling five-second window and treat a
period with no change larger than 5° for at least five minutes as sustained
inactivity, validated against polysomnography and against sleep diaries. Use
`GGIR` on real data.

## The two tables you end up with

Almost every wearable analysis reduces to one or both of these, and it is worth
building them deliberately and saving them (@sec-parquet):

```{r}
#| label: sensor-person-level
person_level <- daily |>
  filter(valid_day) |>
  summarise(
    valid_days = n(),
    wear_hours = mean(wear_minutes) / 60,
    mvpa = mean(mvpa),
    light = mean(light),
    inactive = mean(inactive),
    .by = id
  ) |>
  semi_join(filter(included, included), by = "id") |>
  left_join(select(people, id, age, sex), by = "id")

person_level |>
  summarise(across(c(wear_hours, mvpa, light, inactive),
    list(mean = mean, sd = sd))) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  glimpse()
```

`daily` is the other one: one row per person-day, already built above. Keep
both. The day-level table is what lets you ask within-person questions, and it
is thrown away surprisingly often.

## Analysing the result

```{r}
#| label: sensor-outcomes
#| echo: false
set.seed(11)
# simulated outcomes, generated here so the models below have something to find
person_level <- person_level |>
  mutate(vo2max = round(48 - 0.2 * (age - 45) + 4 * (sex == "male") +
    0.10 * (mvpa - mean(mvpa)) + rnorm(n(), 0, 4), 1))

nights_data <- daily |>
  filter(valid_day) |>
  semi_join(person_level, by = "id") |>
  left_join(summarise(person_level, mvpa_person = mvpa, .by = id), by = "id") |>
  mutate(
    u = rnorm(n_distinct(id), 0, 25)[as.integer(factor(id))],
    sleep_minutes = round(400 + u + 0.6 * (mvpa_person - mean(mvpa_person)) -
      0.3 * (mvpa - mvpa_person) + rnorm(n(), 0, 20))
  )
```

To have something to model, each participant has been given a simulated
`vo2max`, and each valid day a simulated `sleep_minutes` for the night that
followed.

### One number per person

The commonest analysis in the field, and usually the right starting point:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-person-model
model_person <- lm(vo2max ~ I(mvpa / 10) + age + sex + wear_hours,
  data = person_level
)

broom::tidy(model_person, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

Ten more minutes of MVPA per day goes with a higher VO₂max, adjusting for age,
sex and wear time. Everything in @sec-modelling about interpretation applies
unchanged — this is an ordinary linear model that happens to have a device-derived
exposure.

### Days within people

Now a question that only the day-level table can answer: do people sleep
differently after a more active day? The naive approach stacks all the days and
fits one line:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-naive
broom::tidy(lm(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa, data = nights_data), conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

That estimate is a blend of two completely different comparisons: between
people (do active people sleep longer?) and within a person (does this person
sleep longer after their own more active days?). Separate them by splitting the
exposure into a person mean and a deviation from it:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-within-between
#| message: false
library(lme4)

nights_data <- nights_data |>
  mutate(
    mvpa_between = mean(mvpa),
    mvpa_within = mvpa - mean(mvpa),
    .by = id
  )

model_wb <- lmer(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa_within + mvpa_between + (1 | id),
  data = nights_data
)

broom.mixed::tidy(model_wb, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

The two coefficients point in opposite directions. Between people, those who do
more MVPA sleep longer. Within a person, days with more MVPA than usual are
followed by slightly *shorter* sleep. The single pooled estimate was an average
of the two and describes neither.

::: {.callout-important}
## Only the within-person estimate is protected from fixed confounders
`mvpa_within` compares a person with themselves, so everything that does not
change over the week — genetics, age, job, habitual bedtime, personality —
cannot confound it. `mvpa_between` compares different people and is exposed to
all of it.

That makes the within estimate the more trustworthy of the two, but it is not a
causal estimate either: anything that varies day to day (an illness, a holiday,
the weather) can still confound it, and if sleep also affects next-day activity
the arrow may point the other way (@sec-causal). This is the single most
common place where intensive longitudinal data is over-interpreted.
:::

### Centring: which comparison do you get?

The word "centring" covers two operations that do completely different things,
and mixing them up is one of the most common errors in repeated-measures work.

**Grand-mean centring** subtracts one number from everybody: `x - mean(x)`. It
changes what the intercept means, and it makes interaction terms readable
(@sec-modelling). It does **not** change any slope, and it does not separate
anything:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-centring-grand
nights_data <- nights_data |>
  mutate(mvpa_grand = mvpa - mean(mvpa))

c(
  raw = coef(lm(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa, data = nights_data))[["mvpa"]],
  grand_centred = coef(lm(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa_grand, data = nights_data))[["mvpa_grand"]]
) |>
  round(4)
```

Identical, as it must be: shifting a predictor sideways cannot change its
slope.

**Person-mean centring** subtracts a different number from each person: their
own average. That is the operation that splits the exposure into a
within-person part and a between-person part, and it is what the model above
used. `datawizard::demean()` does both halves in one step and names the columns
for you:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-demean
nights_data |>
  select(id, date, mvpa) |>
  datawizard::demean(select = "mvpa", by = "id", verbose = FALSE) |>
  head(3)
```

#### Five ways to fit it, and what each one gives you

```{r}
#| label: sensor-centring-compare
#| message: false
estimate_of <- function(model, term) {
  tidied <- if (inherits(model, "lmerMod")) {
    broom.mixed::tidy(model, effects = "fixed")
  } else {
    broom::tidy(model)
  }
  round(tidied$estimate[tidied$term == term], 3)
}

within_between <- lmer(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa_within + mvpa_between + (1 | id),
  data = nights_data)
mundlak <- lmer(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa + mvpa_between + (1 | id), data = nights_data)

tibble(
  model = c("pooled OLS", "random intercept, raw exposure",
            "within-between", "within-between", "fixed effects for person",
            "Mundlak: raw exposure", "Mundlak: contextual term"),
  estimate = c(
    estimate_of(lm(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa, data = nights_data), "mvpa"),
    estimate_of(lmer(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa + (1 | id), data = nights_data), "mvpa"),
    estimate_of(within_between, "mvpa_within"),
    estimate_of(within_between, "mvpa_between"),
    estimate_of(lm(sleep_minutes ~ mvpa + factor(id), data = nights_data), "mvpa"),
    estimate_of(mundlak, "mvpa"),
    estimate_of(mundlak, "mvpa_between")
  ),
  what_it_estimates = c(
    "a blend of within and between",
    "a partially pooled blend",
    "within-person",
    "between-person",
    "within-person",
    "within-person",
    "between minus within"
  )
)
```

Four things in that table are worth committing to memory.

- **Pooled OLS gives a blend** of two effects that here have opposite signs. It
  is not a compromise between them; it is a number that describes neither.
- **A random intercept on the raw exposure does not fix this.** This is the
  one that catches people out: adding `(1 | id)` handles the *dependence*
  between days, but the slope is still a blend, just a differently weighted
  one.
- **Person fixed effects and the within-between model give exactly the same
  within estimate.** Fixed effects absorb everything stable about a person, at
  the price of being unable to estimate any between-person effect at all.
- **The Mundlak form estimates the same thing in a more testable way.** Its
  second coefficient is the *difference* between the between and within
  effects, so its p-value is a direct test of whether the two differ — which is
  usually the interesting question.

#### Which to use

| Your question | Fit this |
|---|---|
| Do people who move more have better X? | Person-level summary, ordinary regression. You do not need the days. |
| Does a person's X change when they move more than usual? | Within-person centring, or person fixed effects |
| Both, and do they agree? | Within-between model, or the Mundlak form for a direct test |
| Interaction between a day-level and a person-level variable | Within-between, with the interaction on the within part |
| Two timepoints only | A change score; with two waves it is equivalent to fixed effects |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Person means from a handful of days are noisy
`mvpa_between` is each person's average over the few valid days they happened
to provide — here a week at most. That average is an estimate, not a known
value, and a noisy predictor is biased towards zero. So the between-person
estimate is systematically attenuated, and the gap between the within and
between estimates is exaggerated.

The more days per person, the smaller the problem. Seven days is few. If the
within-between contrast is the point of the paper, a multilevel errors-in-
variables model or a reliability-based correction is worth the trouble.
:::

### When during the day?

For the shape of the day rather than its total, fit a smooth curve over time of
day. A **cyclic** spline makes midnight join up with midnight, which an
ordinary spline will not do:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-gam
#| fig-cap: "Modelled time-of-day profile, weekdays versus weekend, from a cyclic spline."
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| message: false
library(mgcv)

profile_data <- wear |>
  filter(worn) |>
  mutate(bin = (min_of_day %/% 10) * 10, weekend = wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6) |>
  summarise(enmo = mean(enmo), .by = c(id, date, bin, weekend)) |>
  summarise(enmo = mean(enmo), .by = c(id, bin, weekend)) |>
  mutate(id = factor(id), weekend = factor(weekend))

model_gam <- bam(
  enmo ~ weekend + s(bin, bs = "cc", k = 20, by = weekend) + s(id, bs = "re"),
  data = profile_data,
  knots = list(bin = c(0, 1440))
)

newdata <- expand_grid(bin = seq(0, 1430, 10), weekend = factor(c(FALSE, TRUE))) |>
  mutate(id = profile_data$id[1])

predictions <- bind_cols(
  newdata,
  as_tibble(predict(model_gam, newdata, se.fit = TRUE, exclude = "s(id)"))
)

predictions |>
  ggplot(aes(bin / 60, fit, colour = weekend, fill = weekend)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = fit - 1.96 * se.fit, ymax = fit + 1.96 * se.fit),
    alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Time of day (h)", y = "Predicted ENMO (mg)", colour = "Weekend", fill = "Weekend")
```

`s(id, bs = "re")` is a random intercept per participant, so the curve is not
dominated by whoever contributed most data, and `exclude = "s(id)"` drops that
term when predicting so the figure shows the population curve.

### The day is only 24 hours long

This is the one statistical issue genuinely specific to this kind of data.
Sleep, sedentary time, light activity and MVPA must add up to the time the
device was worn. They cannot vary independently, so a model that adjusts one
for the others is not asking what it appears to ask.

Having derived the sleep period, we can build the four-part day properly:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-composition
composition <- wear |>
  mutate(night = as.Date(timestamp - hours(12), tz = "Europe/Stockholm")) |>
  left_join(select(sleep, id, night, onset, offset), by = c("id", "night")) |>
  mutate(asleep = !is.na(onset) & timestamp >= onset & timestamp <= offset) |>
  filter(worn) |>
  summarise(
    sleep = sum(asleep),
    sedentary = sum(!asleep & enmo < 50),
    light = sum(!asleep & enmo >= 50 & enmo < 100),
    mvpa = sum(!asleep & enmo >= 100),
    .by = c(id, date)
  ) |>
  semi_join(filter(daily, valid_day), by = c("id", "date")) |>
  summarise(across(c(sleep, sedentary, light, mvpa), mean), .by = id) |>
  left_join(select(person_level, id, vo2max, age, sex), by = "id") |>
  filter(!is.na(vo2max))

composition |>
  summarise(across(c(sleep, sedentary, light, mvpa), \(x) round(mean(x))))

composition |>
  select(sleep, sedentary, light, mvpa) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)
```

The parts are strongly negatively correlated by construction — more of one is
necessarily less of another.

#### Isotemporal substitution

The classic practical answer is an **isotemporal substitution** model
[@mekary2009]: include all the behaviours except one, plus the total. Each coefficient is then the
effect of *replacing* the omitted behaviour with that one, minute for minute.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-substitution
model_sub <- lm(
  vo2max ~ I(mvpa / 10) + I(light / 10) + I(sleep / 10) +
    I((sleep + sedentary + light + mvpa) / 10) + age + sex,
  data = composition
)

broom::tidy(model_sub, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

Sedentary time is left out and the total is in, so the `mvpa` coefficient now
reads: *ten minutes of sedentary time replaced by ten minutes of MVPA, with the
day the same length as before*. That is a question a reader can act on, unlike
"a ten-minute increase in MVPA holding all else constant", which is impossible
by arithmetic.

Compare it with the simple model fitted earlier, though, and notice what
happened. The estimate for MVPA shrank and the confidence interval went from
comfortably positive to spanning zero. Nothing was lost from the data; the
question changed, and the new one is much harder to answer with 24
participants. Light activity and MVPA correlate at 0.94 in this sample, so
asking the model to separate "replace sitting with MVPA" from "replace sitting
with light activity" is asking it to use variation that barely exists.

That is the honest position for substitution models in a small sample: they ask
the right question and often cannot answer it precisely. Report the interval,
resist reading a point estimate the interval does not support, and treat a
substitution analysis as something to power for rather than add at the end.

#### Compositional data analysis

The substitution model is a linear approximation to a problem that is not
linear. Compositional data analysis handles the constraint exactly, and since
@chastin2015 first applied it to accelerometer data it has become the standard
approach for 24-hour movement behaviours. @dumuid2018 is the methodological
reference for this field.

**The idea.** A composition carries information only in the *ratios* between
its parts. Doubling everybody's recording time changes all the minute counts
but changes nothing about how the day is divided. So the analysis should depend
on ratios, and because ratios are multiplicative and awkwardly asymmetric, on
their **logarithms**. Four parts have only three independent pieces of
information, so what you want is three log-ratio coordinates that are free to
take any real value.

Three constructions appear in the literature:

| | Definition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **alr**, additive log-ratio | $\log(x_i / x_D)$ against one chosen part | Simple, but distances are distorted and the choice of reference matters |
| **clr**, centred log-ratio | $\log(x_i / g(\mathbf{x}))$, against the geometric mean | Symmetric and interpretable, but gives $D$ values that sum to zero, so they cannot all go into one regression |
| **ilr**, isometric log-ratio | $D-1$ orthonormal coordinates | What you put in the model |

An **ilr** coordinate is a *balance*: it contrasts the geometric mean of one
group of parts against the geometric mean of another, scaled so the
coordinates are orthonormal. For a split with $r$ parts on one side and $s$ on
the other,

$$
z = \sqrt{\frac{rs}{r+s}} \; \log \frac{g(\text{parts on the } + \text{ side})}{g(\text{parts on the } - \text{ side})}
$$

where $g$ is the geometric mean. That scaling factor is what makes the set
orthonormal, which in turn is what makes the coordinates usable as ordinary
regression predictors.

**Pivot coordinates** are the common default: peel off one part at a time, so
the first coordinate contrasts part 1 against everything else, the second
contrasts part 2 against everything after it, and so on. Put the part you care
about first.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-ilr-function
geomean <- function(x) exp(mean(log(x)))

# ilr coordinates from a sequential binary partition: one row per coordinate,
# one column per part, entries +1 (numerator), -1 (denominator) or 0 (ignored)
ilr_from_sbp <- function(x, sbp) {
  x <- as.matrix(x)
  z <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(x), nrow(sbp),
    dimnames = list(NULL, rownames(sbp)))

  for (k in seq_len(nrow(sbp))) {
    plus <- which(sbp[k, ] == 1)
    minus <- which(sbp[k, ] == -1)
    r <- length(plus)
    s <- length(minus)

    z[, k] <- sqrt(r * s / (r + s)) *
      log(apply(x[, plus, drop = FALSE], 1, geomean) /
        apply(x[, minus, drop = FALSE], 1, geomean))
  }
  as_tibble(z)
}
```

The partition for pivot coordinates on our four parts, with MVPA first:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-ilr-pivot
parts <- c("mvpa", "light", "sedentary", "sleep")

pivot <- rbind(
  mvpa_vs_rest      = c(1, -1, -1, -1),
  light_vs_rest     = c(0,  1, -1, -1),
  sedentary_vs_sleep = c(0,  0,  1, -1)
)
colnames(pivot) <- parts

coords <- ilr_from_sbp(composition[, parts], pivot)

head(coords, 3) |> mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Those three columns go into an ordinary linear model:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-coda-model
coda_data <- bind_cols(composition, coords)

model_coda <- lm(
  vo2max ~ mvpa_vs_rest + light_vs_rest + sedentary_vs_sleep + age + sex,
  data = coda_data
)

broom::tidy(model_coda, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Do not interpret those coefficients directly
A coefficient on a log-ratio coordinate is the change in the outcome per unit
change in a scaled log-ratio, with the other coordinates held fixed. Nobody
can act on that, and the value depends on which partition you chose. Report
**reallocations** instead, and treat the coefficients as machinery.
:::

**Getting an answer back out.** Take the average day, move some minutes from
one part to another, recompute the coordinates, and ask the model what changes.
Because both predictions come from the same linear model, the difference and
its standard error are exact:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-coda-reallocate
mean_day <- composition |>
  summarise(across(all_of(parts), mean))

reallocate <- function(minutes, from, to, model, sbp, average_day) {
  moved <- average_day
  moved[[from]] <- moved[[from]] - minutes
  moved[[to]] <- moved[[to]] + minutes

  # only the coordinates change, so age and sex cancel in the difference
  delta <- as.numeric(ilr_from_sbp(moved[, colnames(sbp)], sbp)) -
    as.numeric(ilr_from_sbp(average_day[, colnames(sbp)], sbp))

  terms <- rownames(sbp)
  estimate <- sum(delta * coef(model)[terms])
  se <- sqrt(drop(t(delta) %*% vcov(model)[terms, terms] %*% delta))

  tibble(
    change = glue::glue("{minutes} min {from} -> {to}"),
    estimate = estimate,
    conf.low = estimate - 1.96 * se,
    conf.high = estimate + 1.96 * se
  )
}

map(c(5, 10, 15, 30), \(m) {
  reallocate(m, "sedentary", "mvpa", model_coda, pivot, mean_day)
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

Two things to read off this. The estimates agree with the linear substitution
model but with a narrower interval, because the compositional model is not
wasting effort on an impossible parametrisation. And the effect is **not
linear in minutes**: thirty minutes is worth less than six times five minutes,
because the ratios change more slowly as you keep adding to an already larger
part. The linear model cannot express that at all.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The choice of partition does not change the fit
Any orthonormal set of coordinates spans the same space, so the model's fitted
values, $R^2$ and every reallocation estimate are identical whichever partition
you choose. Only the individual coefficients change. Pick the partition whose
*structure* matches your question, and never worry that you have chosen the
wrong one in a way that affects the answer.
:::

#### Two compositions, or one with structure

A real question is often about more than one domain: the leisure day and the
working day, or weekdays and weekends. There are three ways to handle that.

**One composition with a structured partition.** This is usually the best
option, and it is what the sequential binary partition was built for. Split the
day into the parts you care about, then write a partition that asks your
questions one at a time:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-domain-composition
domains <- wear |>
  mutate(night = as.Date(timestamp - hours(12), tz = "Europe/Stockholm")) |>
  left_join(select(sleep, id, night, onset, offset), by = c("id", "night")) |>
  filter(worn) |>
  mutate(
    asleep = !is.na(onset) & timestamp >= onset & timestamp <= offset,
    # a crude working day: 08:00-17:00 on weekdays
    at_work = wday(date, week_start = 1) <= 5 & between(min_of_day, 480, 1019),
    part = case_when(
      asleep ~ "sleep",
      at_work & enmo < 50 ~ "work_sed",
      at_work ~ "work_act",
      enmo < 50 ~ "leisure_sed",
      .default = "leisure_act"
    )
  ) |>
  count(id, date, part) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = part, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  semi_join(filter(daily, valid_day), by = c("id", "date")) |>
  summarise(across(-date, mean), .by = id) |>
  left_join(select(person_level, id, vo2max, age, sex), by = "id") |>
  filter(!is.na(vo2max))

domains |>
  summarise(across(c(sleep, work_sed, work_act, leisure_sed, leisure_act),
    \(x) round(mean(x))))
```

```{r}
#| label: sensor-domain-sbp
domain_parts <- c("sleep", "work_sed", "work_act", "leisure_sed", "leisure_act")

domain_sbp <- rbind(
  sleep_vs_wake      = c(1, -1, -1, -1, -1),
  work_vs_leisure    = c(0,  1,  1, -1, -1),
  work_sed_vs_act    = c(0,  1, -1,  0,  0),
  leisure_sed_vs_act = c(0,  0,  0,  1, -1)
)
colnames(domain_sbp) <- domain_parts

model_domain <- lm(
  vo2max ~ sleep_vs_wake + work_vs_leisure + work_sed_vs_act +
    leisure_sed_vs_act + age + sex,
  data = bind_cols(domains, ilr_from_sbp(domains[, domain_parts], domain_sbp))
)
```

Read the partition downwards and it is a set of nested questions: how is the
day split between sleep and waking; within waking, between work and leisure;
within work, between sitting and moving; and within leisure, the same. Each
coordinate answers one of them, and the nesting means they do not compete for
the same variation.

Now reallocations can be asked *inside* a domain, which is what makes this
worth the trouble — moving half an hour of sitting at work is a different
intervention, with a different policy owner, from moving half an hour of
sitting on the sofa:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-domain-reallocate
mean_domain_day <- domains |>
  summarise(across(all_of(domain_parts), mean))

bind_rows(
  reallocate(30, "leisure_sed", "leisure_act", model_domain, domain_sbp, mean_domain_day),
  reallocate(30, "work_sed", "work_act", model_domain, domain_sbp, mean_domain_day),
  reallocate(30, "leisure_sed", "sleep", model_domain, domain_sbp, mean_domain_day),
  reallocate(60, "leisure_sed", "leisure_act", model_domain, domain_sbp, mean_domain_day)
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

**Two separate compositions.** If the domains genuinely are separate — a
leisure composition and a work composition, each with its own parts — you can
build coordinates for each and put both sets in the model, together with the
*total* time in each domain. This is the natural choice when people spend very
different amounts of time at work, because the composition of the working day
and its length are then separate questions. The cost is more coefficients and
more collinearity.

**A subcomposition.** If only one domain matters, analyse it alone: take the
leisure parts, renormalise them to sum to one, and build coordinates from those.
This is clean, but subcompositional analysis discards the information in how
large the domain is, and the ratios within a subcomposition behave differently
from the same ratios in the whole — so say which you did.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Zeros, and where they come from
A log-ratio of zero is undefined, so a single zero part stops the whole
analysis. Our day-level data is full of them — every weekend day has no work
time at all:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-coda-zeros
#| echo: false
cat("zero parts in the day-level composition: ",
  sum(wear |>
    mutate(night = as.Date(timestamp - hours(12), tz = "Europe/Stockholm")) |>
    left_join(select(sleep, id, night, onset, offset), by = c("id", "night")) |>
    filter(worn) |>
    mutate(
      asleep = !is.na(onset) & timestamp >= onset & timestamp <= offset,
      at_work = wday(date, week_start = 1) <= 5 & between(min_of_day, 480, 1019),
      part = case_when(
        asleep ~ "sleep",
        at_work & enmo < 50 ~ "work_sed",
        at_work ~ "work_act",
        enmo < 50 ~ "leisure_sed",
        .default = "leisure_act"
      )
    ) |>
    count(id, date, part) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = part, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
    select(-id, -date) |> as.matrix() == 0),
  "\n")
```

Averaging over the week removes them here, which is one reason person-level
compositions are more common than day-level ones. When they survive, the
options are to merge parts until the zeros disappear, to treat a structural
zero (no work on a Sunday) as genuinely different from a rounded zero (no MVPA
recorded in a day that had some), or to impute the rounded ones with a
dedicated method such as `zCompositions::lrEM()`. Replacing zeros with an
arbitrary small number changes the answer and is not a solution.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Packages
`compositions` and `robCompositions` provide `ilr()`, `clr()`, balance
construction and the matching back-transformations; `ilr_from_sbp()` above is
a transparent version of what they do, and agrees with
`compositions::ilr()` to machine precision when given the same basis.
`zCompositions` handles zeros, and `deltacomp` fits exactly the reallocation
models in this section with less code. For real work, use them. The point of
building it by hand here is that the partition — not the package — is where
your scientific question actually enters.
:::

## Heart rate

Heart rate is the second channel in the example data and behaves differently
from acceleration: it is a *response* rather than a movement count, so it
reflects effort, stress, illness and caffeine as well as activity.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-hr
#| fig-cap: "Heart rate and acceleration for one participant over one day."
#| fig-height: 3.2
sensor |>
  filter(id == "P01", date == as.Date("2026-03-03")) |>
  ggplot(aes(min_of_day / 60)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = enmo), colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = hr), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Time of day (h)", y = "ENMO (mg, grey) and heart rate (bpm, red)")
```

The most robust single number is **resting heart rate**, taken as the lowest
sustained value overnight rather than a single minimum, which would just find
the noisiest minute:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-resting-hr
resting <- sensor |>
  filter(!is.na(hr)) |>
  arrange(id, timestamp) |>
  mutate(rolling_hr = slide_dbl(hr, mean, .before = 29, .complete = TRUE), .by = id) |>
  filter(!is.na(rolling_hr)) |>
  mutate(night = as.Date(timestamp - hours(12), tz = "Europe/Stockholm")) |>
  summarise(resting_hr = min(rolling_hr), .by = c(id, night))

resting |>
  summarise(
    nights = n(),
    mean_resting_hr = round(mean(resting_hr), 1),
    within_person_sd = round(mean(tapply(resting_hr, id, sd)), 2)
  )
```

Intensity from heart rate is usually expressed relative to a person's own
range, because an absolute 130 bpm means different things in different people.
**Heart rate reserve** is the standard device for this: the span between
resting and maximum, with effort expressed as a percentage of it.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-hrr
hr_reserve <- sensor |>
  filter(!is.na(hr)) |>
  summarise(hr_max_observed = quantile(hr, 0.999), .by = id) |>
  left_join(summarise(resting, resting_hr = median(resting_hr), .by = id), by = "id")

hrr <- sensor |>
  filter(!is.na(hr)) |>
  left_join(hr_reserve, by = "id") |>
  mutate(pct_hrr = 100 * (hr - resting_hr) / (hr_max_observed - resting_hr))

hrr |>
  summarise(
    minutes_over_40pct = sum(pct_hrr >= 40),
    minutes_over_60pct = sum(pct_hrr >= 60),
    .by = c(id, date)
  ) |>
  summarise(across(starts_with("minutes"), \(x) round(mean(x), 1)))
```

Two warnings about this. The maximum here is the **observed** maximum over one
week, which depends on whether the person happened to exert themselves; age
prediction equations are the usual alternative and carry an error of around ten
beats per minute for an individual. And the percentage bands that define
moderate and vigorous intensity come from exercise physiology guidelines, so
take the current numbers from the guideline you are citing rather than from
memory.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Heart rate variability needs beat-level data
HRV measures such as RMSSD — the root mean square of successive differences
between beats, in milliseconds — are computed from **inter-beat intervals**,
not from heart rate averaged into epochs. A one-minute mean heart rate cannot
give you HRV, however it is manipulated. If HRV is in your protocol, the device
must export RR intervals, and the measure is sensitive to posture, breathing,
recording length and artefact correction, so the processing choices need
reporting in as much detail as the accelerometer ones.
:::

## Continuous glucose monitoring

CGM data has the same shape — a value every five minutes for a fortnight — and
a well-standardised set of summary measures, which makes it a good example of
how much easier life is when a field agrees on definitions.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-cgm-simulate
set.seed(7)
meals <- tibble(hour = c(8, 12.5, 18.5), size = c(2.2, 2.8, 2.4))

cgm <- expand_grid(
  id = sprintf("C%02d", 1:12),
  date = as.Date("2026-04-01") + 0:13,
  min_of_day = seq(0, 1435, 5)
) |>
  mutate(
    tod = min_of_day / 60,
    baseline = 6.0 + rnorm(n_distinct(id), 0, 1.3)[as.integer(factor(id))],
    response = rnorm(n_distinct(id), 1.2, 0.5)[as.integer(factor(id))]
  ) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(meal_effect = sum(meals$size * response * dnorm(tod, meals$hour + 0.6, 0.75) * 1.9)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(glucose = round(pmax(2.5, baseline + meal_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.35)), 1))
```

The international consensus measures are all proportions of time in named
ranges, plus two summaries [@battelino2019]:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-cgm-metrics
cgm_metrics <- cgm |>
  summarise(
    days = n_distinct(date),
    mean_glucose = mean(glucose),
    cv = 100 * sd(glucose) / mean(glucose),
    time_in_range = 100 * mean(glucose >= 3.9 & glucose <= 10.0),
    time_below = 100 * mean(glucose < 3.9),
    time_above = 100 * mean(glucose > 10.0),
    .by = id
  ) |>
  # Glucose Management Indicator, an estimate of HbA1c (Bergenstal et al. 2018).
  # The published formula takes mg/dL, so convert first.
  mutate(gmi = 3.31 + 0.02392 * (mean_glucose * 18.018))

cgm_metrics |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_glucose)) |>
  head(5)
```

The consensus targets for most adults with diabetes are time in range above
70%, time below 3.9 mmol/L under 4%, time above 10.0 mmol/L under 25%, and a
coefficient of variation at or below 36%, computed over at least 14 days with
the sensor active at least 70% of the time [@battelino2019]. Checking data
sufficiency before computing anything is the same `count()` habit as before:

```{r}
#| label: sensor-cgm-sufficiency
cgm |>
  summarise(readings = n(), .by = id) |>
  mutate(
    expected = 14 * 288, # 288 five-minute readings per day
    completeness = round(100 * readings / expected, 1)
  ) |>
  summarise(min_completeness = min(completeness), n = n())
```

The standard figure is the **ambulatory glucose profile**: all days overlaid as
a median with percentile bands, which shows when during the day the problems
happen rather than just how often.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-agp
#| fig-cap: "Ambulatory glucose profile for one participant: median with 25th-75th and 5th-95th percentile bands across 14 days."
#| fig-height: 3.4
cgm |>
  filter(id == "C01") |>
  summarise(
    median = median(glucose),
    q25 = quantile(glucose, 0.25), q75 = quantile(glucose, 0.75),
    q05 = quantile(glucose, 0.05), q95 = quantile(glucose, 0.95),
    .by = min_of_day
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(min_of_day / 60)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 3.9, ymax = 10,
    alpha = 0.12, fill = "forestgreen") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Time of day (h)", y = "Glucose (mmol/L)")
```

The `iglu` package implements these metrics and several dozen more, and is
worth using instead of writing your own once you move past the basics.

## Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## The ones that cost people a paper
- **Analysing minutes as if they were independent.** 250,000 rows is not
  250,000 observations. Aggregate to the level of your question, or model the
  structure.
- **Letting non-wear become zeroes.** The single most common serious error, and
  it biases activity downwards exactly in the least compliant participants.
- **Comparing across devices, wear locations or cut-points.** Hip and wrist are
  not interchangeable, and neither are counts and ENMO.
- **Reverse causation.** Illness, pain and low mood reduce activity. A
  cross-sectional association between activity and health status says little
  about direction (@sec-causal).
- **Reactivity.** People move more in the first day or two of wearing a device.
  Some protocols discard day one; whatever you do, say so.
- **Fishing across derived measures.** Totals, bouts, intensities, timing,
  fragmentation, five cut-points: the number of outcomes you can derive from one
  week of data is effectively unlimited. Pre-specify, and report what you tried.
- **A stated precision the method cannot support.** "41.3 minutes of MVPA" from
  a cut-point with a 30% uncertainty band is false precision.
:::

## Making it reproducible

Sensor pipelines are long, slow and run many times, which is exactly the
situation a pipeline tool is built for (@sec-pipelines). Three things pay off
immediately:

- **Keep the raw files read-only** and write every derived level to its own
  file. You will re-run the epoch-to-day step many times and the raw-to-epoch
  step rarely.
- **Store intermediate tables as Parquet** (@sec-parquet). It keeps column types
  and reads far faster than CSV at this size.
- **Make the pipeline explicit** with `targets`, so that changing a cut-point
  re-runs the classification and everything after it, and nothing else.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# _targets.R, in outline
list(
  tar_target(raw_files, list.files("data-raw", full.names = TRUE), format = "file"),
  tar_target(epochs, read_and_summarise(raw_files), pattern = map(raw_files)),
  tar_target(wear, detect_nonwear(epochs, min_length = 60)),
  tar_target(daily, summarise_days(wear, mvpa_cutpoint = 100)),
  tar_target(person, summarise_people(daily, min_valid_days = 4)),
  tar_target(report, tarchetypes::tar_quarto(report.qmd))
)
```

Writing it this way also makes the sensitivity analysis trivial: a cut-point is
an argument, so a second branch with a different value costs one line.

## Packages worth knowing

| Package | For |
|---|---|
| `GGIR` | The standard open pipeline for raw accelerometer files: reading, calibration, non-wear, sleep and activity metrics |
| `read.gt3x`, `actilifecounts` | Reading ActiGraph `.gt3x` files and producing counts |
| `iglu` | CGM metrics, including everything in the consensus list |
| `slider`, `zoo` | Rolling windows |
| `lubridate`, `hms`, `clock` | Timestamps, time zones, times of day |
| `arrow`, `duckdb` | Data that no longer fits in memory (@sec-parquet) |
| `mgcv` | Smooth time-of-day and dose-response curves |
| `lme4`, `nlme` | Days within people |
| `compositions`, `deltacomp` | 24-hour compositional analysis and substitution |
| `targets` | Keeping the pipeline honest (@sec-pipelines) |

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check yourself**

Why is non-wear detected from a *run* of low values rather than from single low
minutes?
`r longmcq(c(
  "Because single minutes are never low",
  answer = "Because sleep also produces low values, and only a long flat run distinguishes a removed device",
  "Because devices only record once an hour",
  "To reduce the file size"
))`

A participant's device is in a drawer for six hours. If you do not detect it,
their daily MVPA will be
`r mcq(c("too high", answer = "too low", "unchanged", "impossible to say"))`

In the within/between model, which coefficient is protected from confounding by
things that do not change over the study week, such as age and occupation?
`r mcq(c("the between-person coefficient", answer = "the within-person coefficient", "both", "neither"))`

You adjust a model for sedentary, light and MVPA time at the same time, without
including total wear time. The problem is
`r longmcq(c(
  "the model will not converge",
  answer = "the behaviours sum to the wear time, so the coefficients do not describe the substitution you think they do",
  "sedentary time is always measured with error",
  "nothing; this is the recommended approach"
))`

Mean heart rate per minute is enough to compute RMSSD. `r torf(FALSE)`

Moving the MVPA cut-point from 100 to 120 mg changes average MVPA in this
dataset by roughly
`r mcq(c("less than 1%", "about 5%", answer = "a fifth, downwards", "it has no effect"))`
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exercise 1: a bout definition with tolerance

The bouts above end the moment a single minute drops below the threshold. Most
published definitions are more forgiving: a short dip does not end the bout.
Implement that, and see how much it matters.

1. Start from `wear` and flag MVPA minutes as before.
2. Find the runs with `consecutive_id()`, and record how long each run is.
3. Treat an *inactive* run of at most two minutes as part of the bout, then
   find the runs again on the revised flag.
4. Keep the runs of at least 10 minutes and compare the total bouted minutes
   per day with the strict definition.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: ex1-sensor-sol
bridged <- wear |>
  arrange(id, timestamp) |>
  mutate(active = worn & enmo >= 100) |>
  mutate(run = consecutive_id(active), .by = c(id, date)) |>
  mutate(run_length = n(), .by = c(id, date, run)) |>
  # a gap of at most two minutes does not end a bout
  mutate(active_tolerant = active | run_length <= 2) |>
  mutate(run2 = consecutive_id(active_tolerant), .by = c(id, date)) |>
  summarise(active_tolerant = first(active_tolerant), length = n(),
    .by = c(id, date, run2)) |>
  filter(active_tolerant, length >= 10)

bind_rows(
  strict = bouts_found |> summarise(minutes = sum(length), .by = c(id, date)),
  tolerant = bridged |> summarise(minutes = sum(length), .by = c(id, date)),
  .id = "definition"
) |>
  summarise(mean_bouted_minutes = round(mean(minutes), 1), .by = definition)
```

The tolerant definition finds about a third more bouted minutes, because single
dips no longer split one bout into two short ones that then fail the ten-minute
rule.

Neither number is the truth. The point is that the gap between them is larger
than most of the effects people report, and that it comes entirely from a
decision taken in code. The same applies to the ten-minute minimum itself: the
2018 US physical activity guidelines dropped the bout requirement altogether,
so a paper reporting bouted MVPA and one reporting total MVPA are not measuring
the same thing.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Exercise 2: what does non-wear pretend to be?

Non-wear is not a neutral gap. Find out what it turns into if you do not
detect it.

1. From `wear`, compute for each person-day the inactive minutes (ENMO below
   50) two ways: counting every minute, and counting only worn minutes.
2. How many minutes a day of false inactivity does the first version invent?
3. Compute each participant's average MVPA and their average inflation, and
   correlate the two. Who is most affected?
4. Also correlate average wear time with average MVPA across participants.
   What does that imply for a model that does not adjust for wear time?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| label: ex2-sensor-sol
bias <- wear |>
  summarise(
    wear_minutes = sum(worn),
    inactive_all = sum(enmo < 50), # non-wear counted as inactivity
    inactive_worn = sum(worn & enmo < 50), # non-wear excluded
    mvpa = sum(worn & enmo >= 100),
    .by = c(id, date)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    wear = mean(wear_minutes),
    mvpa = mean(mvpa),
    inflation = mean(inactive_all - inactive_worn),
    .by = id
  )

bias |>
  summarise(
    mean_inflation = round(mean(inflation), 1),
    max_inflation = round(max(inflation), 1)
  )

bias |>
  summarise(
    inflation_vs_mvpa = round(cor(inflation, mvpa), 2),
    wear_vs_mvpa = round(cor(wear, mvpa), 2)
  )
```

Undetected non-wear becomes **sedentary time**, not missing time: on average
about 170 extra minutes a day of inactivity that nobody actually spent sitting.
It barely touches MVPA, because a device in a drawer does not produce high
values — which is why an analysis of MVPA can look fine while the sedentary
analysis built from the same file is badly wrong.

Worse, the inflation is not spread evenly. It correlates negatively with MVPA,
so the least active participants gain the most fake sedentary time, which
exaggerates the very contrast the study is about.

The last correlation is the one to remember: wear time and MVPA are positively
correlated across participants. People who wear the device more also move more.
A model that does not account for wear time cannot tell those two things apart,
which is why `wear_hours` is in the person-level model earlier in the chapter.
:::
:::

## More information

- [GGIR documentation](https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/) — the reference pipeline
  for raw accelerometer data, with a detailed account of each processing step
- [iglu](https://irinagain.github.io/iglu/) — CGM metrics, with the consensus
  definitions implemented
- [slider](https://slider.r-lib.org/) — rolling windows, including index-aware
  ones
- @migueles2017 — a systematic review of accelerometer collection and
  processing criteria, and the usual source for valid-day conventions
- @doherty2017 — how a very large study processes wrist accelerometer data
- @vanhees2015 — the open sleep-detection method behind `GGIR`
- @dumuid2018 — compositional data analysis for movement behaviours, and
  @chastin2015 for the first application of it to this kind of data
- @battelino2019 — the international consensus on CGM targets and reporting
